items.passage: Because a snail whose shell coils in the direction opposite to that of its neighbors has difficulty mating, biologists have long been puzzled by how sinistral, or left-coiling, species originate among terrestrial snails, the great majority of which are dextral, or right-coiling. Investigating Iwasaki’s snail-eater (Pareas iwasakii), a snake endemic to Japan’s Ryukyu Islands, biologist Masaki Hoso and colleagues discovered that its right mandible bears far more teeth than its left, an asymmetry well suited to extracting snails from dextral shells. In feeding trials, the snakes frequently failed when attacking sinistral snails.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes research on a predator’s anatomy that explains why the predator has become more abundant on islands where most snails coil to the right.
It describes a study of a snake’s teeth and feeding behavior that was designed to determine whether snails with opposite coiling directions are able to mate.
It describes research on a predator that suggests a possible explanation for how a rare trait could become established in that predator’s prey.
It presents findings showing that a snake’s feeding habits have made left-coiling snails more common than right-coiling snails on Japan’s Ryukyu Islands.
items.explanation: The first sentence raises a question: because a snail that coils the opposite way has trouble mating, it is unclear how left-coiling (sinistral) species ever arise. The rest of the text reports that a snail-eating snake has teeth arranged for right-coiling shells and often fails when it attacks sinistral snails. Read together, these findings point to a possible answer: snails that coil the rare way may survive such attacks, which could help that trait become established. Choice C states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text does describe the snake’s jaw, but it says nothing about how common the snake has become anywhere; the findings bear on the snails, not on the snake’s numbers.

B.why_wrong: The study did examine the snake’s teeth and feeding, but the text never says it tested whether snails can mate. Mating difficulty is the background the first sentence states, not the study’s question.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that the snakes often fail against left-coiling snails; it reports nothing about how common either kind of snail is on the islands, and it notes that most land snails coil to the right.

sources.what: Hoso, Asami and Hori (2007): Pareas iwasakii has more teeth on the right mandible and is much less adept at preying on sinistral snails

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolutionary biology). Key C. Span of the purpose: question (sentence 1) plus finding (sentences 2 and 3); the answer to the question is left implicit. Key parts: 2 (research on a predator; a possible explanation for a rare prey trait). Section 6 checks: key 23 words; options 21 to 26 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A and B (2 of 3). Smaller details simplified: tooth counts given only as 'far more'.
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose: the key names the research and the question it bears on ("a possible explanation", "could become established")
the answer is never stated: the student joins the opening question to the last sentence
two distractors (A, B) keep a true first clause about the research and fail in the later clause; D overreaches from a possible explanation to a demonstrated change in which snails are more common
abstract key: no passage nouns (snake, snail, teeth, sinistral) appear in it

fixes: D rewritten from a reversal (a preference for left-coiling snails, killed by one fact) to an overreach near miss (the snake has made left-coiling snails more common on the islands); why_wrong, recipe and band7_moves updated
stale note on tooth counts corrected to the passage wording
checks: core claim confirmed against the source

band7.why: 82cb7dda shape: a hedged dual purpose ("suggests a possible explanation ... could become established") whose answer the text never states; the student joins the opening puzzle to the last sentence. Key shares no content words with the passage. After the fix, B (study aimed at mating) and D (prevalence overreach) are near misses and A keeps a true first clause; four checks met (key 23 words, 2 parts, 2 first-half matches).

items.passage: Roughly every fourteen months, GPS stations on Vancouver Island briefly reverse their usual northeastward drift, indicating that the deep portion of the Cascadia subduction zone, where one tectonic plate descends beneath another, has slipped gradually over several weeks. Because this slow slip generated no detectable earthquakes, geophysicists initially considered it silent. Comparing six years of records, however, seismologists Garry Rogers and Herb Dragert determined that each slip episode coincided, in both timing and location, with a faint, persistent seismic signal known as tremor, a correspondence they proposed could serve as an indicator of accumulating stress on the fault.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It summarizes research revealing that a process once thought to be undetectable by seismometers is in fact accompanied by a distinctive signal that might be useful for monitoring a fault.
It summarizes research revealing that slow slip is accompanied by a distinctive seismic signal and suggests that the signal can be used to predict when the next major earthquake will occur.
It explains how GPS stations track the gradual movement of tectonic plates and why that method is more reliable than measurements made by seismometers.
It describes how researchers determined that tremor originating near the surface causes the deep part of a fault to slip over a period of weeks.
items.explanation: The text first describes slow slip, which GPS stations reveal but which was thought to be “silent” because it produced no detectable earthquakes. It then reports that Rogers and Dragert found a faint seismic signal, tremor, accompanying each slip episode, and that they proposed this pairing as an indicator of stress on the fault. So the text summarizes research showing that a supposedly silent process has a seismic signature that might help in monitoring a fault, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first clause true, overreach in the later clause (BROAD)
B.why_wrong: The researchers proposed the pairing as an indicator of accumulating stress; the text never says it can predict when an earthquake will occur.

C.recipe: first part partly true, invented comparison (INV)
C.why_wrong: GPS stations do reveal the slip, but the text does not explain how they work or rank them against seismometers; seismic records are what revealed the tremor.

D.why_wrong: The text says tremor coincided with slip in time and place; it never says tremor causes the slip, and it places both deep in the subduction zone, not near the surface.

sources.what: Rogers and Dragert (2003, Science): tremor coincides in time and place with slow slip episodes on the Cascadia subduction zone; episodic tremor and slip proposed as an indicator of stress loading

items.notes: Area: natural science (geophysics). Key A. Key parts: 2 (a supposedly undetectable process has a signal; the signal might help monitor a fault). Section 6 checks: key 30 words; options 24 to 31 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: B and C (2 of 3). Recurrence given as 'roughly every fourteen months' (the paper reports 13 to 16 months).
band7_moves: dual purpose with a hedge ("might be useful for monitoring")
B is a near miss on the second clause: stress indicator versus earthquake prediction
two distractors (B, C) open with a true first part and fail later; D swaps cause and effect
abstract key: "a process once thought to be undetectable by seismometers" for the slow slip, with no passage wording carried over

fixes: source URL (science.gc.ca, now 404) replaced with the Science DOI; abstract confirms six years of data, tremor matching slip in time and place, ETS proposed as an indicator of stress loading
stale note on the recurrence interval corrected
checks: core claim confirmed against the source

band7.why: 82cb7dda shape: dual purpose with a hedge ("might be useful for monitoring"), key abstracted from "silent"; B shares the key's first half and fails only on stress indicator versus earthquake prediction. C and D are easier kills, as A and B are in the model. Key 30 words, mean option length about 27.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Maria Edgeworth’s 1801 novel Belinda. Belinda Portman, a young woman, has come to stay at the London home of Lady Delacour, who is celebrated in fashionable society for her wit and gaiety.

A short time after her arrival at Lady Delacour’s, Belinda began to see through the thin veil with which politeness covers domestic misery. Abroad [in public], and at home, Lady Delacour was two different persons. Abroad she appeared all life, spirit, and good humour—at home, listless, fretful, and melancholy; she seemed like a spoiled actress off the stage, over-stimulated by applause, and exhausted by the exertions of supporting a fictitious character.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To reveal that Lady Delacour resents Belinda for having seen through her public manner
To suggest that Lady Delacour was once a successful actress who now misses performing
To convey Belinda’s disappointment on finding that life in Lady Delacour’s home is much duller than she had expected
To present a character’s discovery that another character’s public liveliness conceals private unhappiness
items.explanation: The context line says Lady Delacour is celebrated for her wit and gaiety. Soon after arriving, Belinda “began to see through the thin veil” of politeness: in public Lady Delacour is “all life, spirit, and good humour,” but at home she is “listless, fretful, and melancholy,” like an actress exhausted by playing a part. So the text presents Belinda’s discovery that her host’s public liveliness hides private misery, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: Nothing shows Lady Delacour noticing Belinda’s discovery, much less resenting it.

B.why_wrong: Lady Delacour only “seemed like” an actress; the comparison describes her exhausting public performance, not a former career.

C.recipe: feeling given to the wrong character (SWAP)
C.why_wrong: The misery described is Lady Delacour’s; the text does not say Belinda is disappointed or that she finds the house dull.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Belinda, chapter 1, in Edgeworth’s Tales and Novels, vol. 3); novel first published 1801

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1801, public domain). Adapted only by printing the source’s “misery.--Abroad” as two sentences and adding the gloss [in public] (“abroad” here means out in society). Key D. Band 6 hard: the key is an abstract two-part purpose (a discovery; public liveliness versus private unhappiness), and C tempts by giving the unhappiness to the observer. Not a clone of Jane Eyre (03c9f327): there the contrast is within the narrator; here an observer discovers it in someone else.

checks: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 9455: exact except the marked adaptation (".--Abroad" printed as two sentences, gloss [in public]); accepted because CB adapts the same way: bracketed glosses (d9e55268 mercantile [general store], d5600e74 Papá [his father]) and silent punctuation and wording changes in ea971260 (Alcott: "her" to "Polly", "did n't" to "didn't", a semicolon join cut to a period) and 0a04cac5 (Austen: "chusing" to "choosing")

band7.why: P_lit band-6 pattern (03c9f327): a two-part public versus private contrast in pre-1810 prose with an abstract key; C hands the unhappiness to the observer. Distractors A and B fall on one fact each, so not 7.

items.passage: Histories of photography have long centered on a handful of European inventors, chiefly Louis Daguerre and William Henry Fox Talbot, who publicized their processes in 1839. In the Brazilian town of Campinas, however, <u>the French-born artist Hercule Florence had by 1833 fixed images produced by a camera obscura onto paper coated with silver salts</u>, and in his notebooks he called the process “photographie.” Florence’s experiments attracted little attention until historian Boris Kossoy examined the notebooks in the 1970s and concluded that photography had been discovered independently in Brazil, in isolation from the work then under way in Europe.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a case that, according to the text, later led a historian to conclude that Daguerre and Talbot did not deserve credit for their processes.
It describes a case that, according to the text, later led a historian to conclude that a technology arose separately in more than one place.
It describes an early experiment that, as the text goes on to explain, shaped the processes that Daguerre and Talbot publicized in 1839.
It explains why historians of photography overlooked Florence’s notebooks until the 1970s.
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the usual account, in which photography begins with Daguerre and Talbot in Europe. The underlined portion describes Florence’s photographic work in Brazil by 1833. The final sentence explains what was made of it: Kossoy concluded that photography had been discovered independently in Brazil, apart from the work in Europe. So the underlined case is the one that led a historian to conclude that the technology arose separately in more than one place, as choice B says.

A.recipe: first clause true, overreach in the later clause (BROAD)
A.why_wrong: Kossoy concluded that Florence’s discovery was independent of the European work, not that Daguerre and Talbot deserve no credit; the text gives no reason to deny them credit.

C.why_wrong: The final sentence says Florence’s work attracted little attention and developed “in isolation from the work then under way in Europe,” so it cannot have shaped Daguerre’s and Talbot’s processes.

D.why_wrong: The underlined portion says what Florence achieved, not why his notebooks were overlooked; the following sentence reports only that his experiments attracted little attention.

sources.what: Hercule Florence’s photographic work in Campinas (1833) and Boris Kossoy’s research establishing it as an independent discovery

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (history of photography). Key B. Span role: means (a single case whose significance is given only in the following sentence). Key parts: 2 (a case; it led a historian to a conclusion about independent invention). Section 6 checks: key 25 words; mean option length 21.5 words; compound clause marker in key: yes ("according to the text"); distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A and C (2 of 3). Third F_example shape, distinct from our extent-number (Hawaiian newspapers) and complicates-a-view (Norman Lewis) items: here the case is evidence for a scholar’s generalization stated after it.
band7_moves: the span is a single case, a means; its job is fixed by the sentence after it (deciding clue after the span)
key of two clauses: the case, then what a historian concluded from it, stated abstractly ("a technology arose separately in more than one place")
A and C keep the key’s true first clause and fail later: a credit claim the text never makes, and an influence the final sentence rules out
D answers a nearby question (the following sentence’s content)

fixes: key B: "emerged independently" changed to "arose separately" so the key no longer repeats the passage's "discovered independently"; explanation and band7_moves updated
checks: core claim confirmed against the source

band7.why: F_example band-7 recipe (2e744883, 9b01bcf4): the span is a single case whose job is fixed only by the next sentence; key of two clauses with "according to the text", now with no passage echo; A and C keep the true first clause and fail later (credit claim, influence the final sentence rules out); D is the neighbor-sentence trap.

items.passage: Kathleen Collins completed Losing Ground in 1982, becoming one of the first African American women to write and direct a feature-length drama. The film follows Sara, a philosophy professor investigating the nature of ecstatic experience, through a summer in which her marriage to a painter deteriorates; unusually for American cinema of the period, it treats a Black woman’s intellectual life as its central subject. Collins died in 1988, before the film secured a distributor, and it remained largely unseen until a restoration decades later brought it widespread critical acclaim.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To introduce a film, identify what set it apart, and explain why few people saw it for many years
To argue that Losing Ground influenced many later films about the careers of women scholars
To compare the critical reception of Losing Ground in 1982 with its reception after it was restored
To describe the obstacles that prevented Black women filmmakers of the 1980s from finding distributors for their work
items.explanation: The text introduces Losing Ground and its place among early features by Black women, then describes what set the film apart (it centers a Black woman’s intellectual life), and finally explains why it was little seen: Collins died before it found a distributor, and it reached wide audiences only after its restoration. Choice A covers all three parts.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about later films, and it does not argue for the film’s influence.

C.why_wrong: The film was barely screened in 1982, and the text describes no reception from that time to compare with later acclaim.

D.why_wrong: The text explains why one film lacked a distributor (Collins died first); it does not discuss obstacles facing Black women filmmakers in general.

sources.what: Losing Ground (1982), written and directed by Kathleen Collins; plot; Collins’s death in 1988; restoration and later release

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (film). Key A. Plan asked band 7, but P_profile has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md), so written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md. Three-part key like 3.18; distractors BROAD, INV, STANCE as in the band-6 models.

checks: core claim confirmed against the source

items.passage: Ecologist Madhav Gadgil contended that conservation in India had too often been directed by distant government agencies and scientific specialists, who regarded the farmers, herders, and fishers living nearest to forests and rivers as threats to be excluded rather than as communities possessing detailed knowledge of local flora and fauna. Beginning in the 1990s, Gadgil helped establish People’s Biodiversity Registers, through which villagers, collaborating with local schools and colleges, documented the species surrounding them, the purposes those species served, and the ways their populations had changed over time.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes how a scientist surveyed the plants and animals of a region and then explains why villagers were reluctant to share their knowledge with him.
The text presents a scientist’s criticism of the way conservation was carried out and then explains why government agencies rejected the alternative he proposed.
The text describes a project in which villagers recorded local species and then presents a scientist’s argument that such records are less reliable than experts’ surveys.
The text presents a scientist’s objection to how conservation was practiced in his country and then describes an effort he helped lead to address that objection.
items.explanation: The first sentence gives Gadgil’s criticism: conservation in India was run by distant agencies and experts who treated local people as threats rather than as holders of knowledge. The second sentence describes the People’s Biodiversity Registers he helped establish, in which villagers themselves recorded local species, an effort that answers that criticism. Choice D describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: Gadgil did not conduct a survey in the text, and no villager is described as reluctant; the registers were compiled by villagers.

B.recipe: first move right, later move invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text presents his criticism but then describes the registers being established, not rejected by government agencies.

C.why_wrong: The criticism comes first, and Gadgil champions local knowledge; he does not call villagers’ records less reliable than experts’ surveys.

sources.what: Madhav Gadgil’s critique of centralized, expert-led conservation and his People’s Biodiversity Registers
Gadgil et al. (2000, Ecological Applications): People’s Biodiversity Registers prepared in India from 1995 by schools, colleges and NGOs working with village communities

items.passage: Since 2012, Inuk vocalist Tanya Tagaq has performed a live score for Nanook of the North, a 1922 silent film depicting an Inuit family in northern Quebec. Rather than following written notation, Tagaq improvises beside the screen, drawing on the techniques of Inuit throat singing as she growls, gasps, and sings in response to the projected images, accompanied by a violinist and a percussionist. Reviewing a 2015 performance, a critic for San Francisco Classical Voice asserted that Tagaq had reclaimed the film for Inuit audiences, rendering it less an ethnographic study than a portrait of Arctic survival.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a silent film, explains why the film was controversial when it was first released, and then describes a musician’s effort to correct its errors.
It presents a project that pairs live music with a film, outlines the method the performer uses, and then explains why some reviewers found the improvisation distracting.
It introduces a performance project, describes how the performer approaches it, and then reports a critic’s view of what the performance accomplishes.
It introduces a performer, explains how she learned the techniques of throat singing, and then describes how Inuit audiences have responded to her music.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Tagaq’s live score for Nanook of the North. The second describes her approach: she improvises, drawing on throat singing, with two accompanists. The third reports a critic’s assessment that she reclaimed the film for Inuit audiences. Choice C names these three moves in order.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no history of the film’s first reception and does not say Tagaq corrects errors in it.

B.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The review quoted is favorable; no reviewer is said to find the improvisation distracting.

D.recipe: second move invented, third a word hook (INV/LIT)
D.why_wrong: The text does not say how Tagaq learned throat singing, and “for Inuit audiences” is a critic’s view of the performance, not an account of how Inuit audiences responded.

sources.what: Tagaq’s improvised live score for Nanook of the North; San Francisco Classical Voice review saying she reclaimed the film for Inuit audiences

items.passage:
The following text is from Susan Ferrier’s 1818 novel Marriage. Lady Juliana, a young woman accustomed to fashionable society in London, is traveling with her husband to his family’s home, Glenfern Castle, in the Scottish Highlands.

But she remembered the Duchess had said the inns and roads were execrable; and the face of the country, as well as the lower orders of people, frightful; but what signified those things? There were balls, and sailing parties, and rowing matches, and shooting parties, and fishing parties, and parties of every description; and the certainty of being recompensed by the festivities of Glenfern Castle, reconciled her to the ruggedness of the approach.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the hardships that most travelers of the early nineteenth century faced on the roads of the Scottish Highlands
To show that a character’s hopes for amusement make her willing to endure an unpleasant journey
To reveal that a character regrets her decision to visit her husband’s family
To explain why a character doubts what the Duchess told her about the region
items.explanation: Lady Juliana recalls being told that the inns and roads are “execrable” and the country “frightful,” but she dismisses this (“what signified those things?”) because she expects balls and “parties of every description” at Glenfern Castle. The certainty of those festivities “reconciled her to the ruggedness of the approach.” So the text shows her hopes for amusement making her willing to put up with a hard journey, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports what one character remembers hearing about the roads; it is about her attitude, not about what most travelers faced.

C.why_wrong: She is reconciled to the journey by the pleasures she expects; nothing suggests regret.

D.why_wrong: She accepts what the Duchess said and simply decides it does not matter; she never questions it.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Marriage, volume 1, chapter 5); novel first published 1818

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1818, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from the Project Gutenberg text. Key B. Medium: older prose; the key requires reading “what signified those things?” as dismissal.

checks: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact

items.passage:
The following text is from Mary Webb’s 1924 novel Precious Bane. Prue Sarn, the narrator, lives on her family’s farm in rural England in the early 1800s. She has just described a moment of intense, unexplained joy that once came to her while she sat alone in the farmhouse attic.

Though the visitation came but seldom, the taste of it was in the attic all the while. I had but to creep in there, and hear the bees making their murmur, and smell the woody, o’er-sweet scent of kept apples, and hear the leaves rasping softly on the window-frame, and watch the twisted grey twigs on the sky, and I’d remember it and forget all else.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the household tasks the narrator performs in the attic each day
To convey the narrator’s fear that a joyful experience will never be repeated
To explain why the narrator prefers the company of animals to that of people
To convey how a place helps the narrator recall a rare and treasured experience
items.explanation: The “visitation” is the moment of joy described in the context line. Though it came “but seldom,” its “taste” stayed in the attic: whenever the narrator creeps in and hears the bees, smells the stored apples, and watches the twigs against the sky, she remembers it “and forget[s] all else.” So the text conveys how the attic lets her call back a rare and treasured experience, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The narrator goes to the attic to listen, smell, and watch, not to do chores; no tasks are mentioned.

B.why_wrong: The text says the experience came seldom, but it expresses no fear that it will never return; the attic keeps its “taste” with her.

C.why_wrong: The bees are one of the sounds that help her remember; the text compares no animals with people.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Precious Bane, book 1); novel first published 1924

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1924; public domain in the United States). Excerpt copied exactly from the Project Gutenberg text, dialect kept (o’er-sweet, I’d). Key D. The context line supplies what “the visitation” refers to, as CB context lines do.

checks: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact

items.passage: Most animals’ eyes consist of soft tissue, but the West Indian fuzzy chiton (Acanthopleura granulata), a mollusk that clings to rocks along Caribbean shorelines, possesses hundreds of tiny eyes embedded in the hard plates protecting its back. In 2015 materials scientist Ling Li and colleagues reported that <u>the lens of each eye consists of aragonite, the same mineral that composes the surrounding plates, with its crystals aligned so that light passes through without being substantially scattered</u>. The eyes come at a cost, however: the plates are mechanically weaker where the eyes are located.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes features of the chiton’s lenses that allow them to transmit light clearly.
It explains why the chiton’s plates are weaker in some places than in others.
It identifies the method the researchers used to count the eyes on each of the chiton’s plates.
It presents a hypothesis about why chitons evolved eyes when most other mollusks did not.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces the puzzle of a mollusk with eyes set in hard plates. The underlined portion explains what the lenses are made of and how they work: they are aragonite, and their crystals are aligned so that light passes through without much scattering. So it describes the features that let these mineral lenses transmit light clearly, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The weakness of the plates is reported in the last sentence; the underlined portion is about the lenses themselves.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no counting method; it says only that the chiton has hundreds of eyes.

D.why_wrong: The underlined portion reports what the lenses are made of; it offers no account of why chitons evolved eyes, and other mollusks are not discussed.

sources.what: Li et al. (2015, Science): chiton eyes with aragonite lenses that form images; aligned crystal grains reduce scattering; local weakening of the armor

items.notes: Area: natural science (materials science, zoology). Key A. F_method: the span is a mechanism, as in 2.14 and 2.15.

checks: core claim confirmed against the source

items.passage: Bronze is produced by combining copper with tin, but tin ores are rare in the eastern Mediterranean, so the origin of the tin consumed by Bronze Age societies there has long remained uncertain. In 2019 archaeologist Daniel Berger and colleagues analyzed tin ingots from the thirteenth and twelfth centuries BCE that had been recovered from shipwrecks off Israel’s coast. <u>The ingots’ chemical and isotopic signatures closely matched those of tin ores from Cornwall and Devon, in southwestern England.</u> That correspondence suggests that, more than 3,000 years ago, tin was traveling from the far northwest of Europe to the eastern Mediterranean.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the method the researchers used to determine the age of the ingots mentioned in the previous sentence.
It presents a hypothesis about the ingots’ origin that is rejected in the following sentence.
It reports a result that provides the basis for the conclusion stated in the following sentence.

items.passage: Ethnomusicologist Thomas Turino distinguishes presentational performance, in which musicians play for an audience, from participatory performance, whose main goal is to involve as many people as possible in making music. items.passage: Many dog owners are convinced that a dog that lowers its head and averts its gaze after misbehaving is expressing guilt. That interpretation may be premature. Upon returning, some owners were informed, not always accurately, that their dogs had eaten the treat, and those owners scolded them. The so-called guilty look appeared most frequently when dogs were scolded, regardless of whether they had actually disobeyed.

items.passage: Ice is remarkably slippery even beneath a person standing still, yet the reason has long been debated. The familiar explanation, in which pressure from a skate or shoe melts the surface into a lubricating film, fails: a person exerts far too little pressure to lower ice’s melting point appreciably. Frictional heating is also an unlikely cause, since in experiments by physicist Daniel Bonn and colleagues, slipperiness remained constant across sliding speeds, contrary to what frictional melting would predict. More promising is Bonn’s proposal that loosely bound surface molecules roll freely, like tiny ball bearings.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a familiar property of a substance, explains why two proposed causes of it fall short, and then concludes that the property may never be fully explained.
It introduces an everyday phenomenon, gives reasons for doubting two accounts of it, and then presents a third account that the author finds more convincing.
It introduces a phenomenon, presents two competing accounts of it that the author considers equally likely, and then describes an experiment designed to decide between them.
It introduces a phenomenon, explains why two accounts of it are inadequate, and then reports experiments that established a third account as correct.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces the phenomenon: ice is slippery, and the reason has long been debated. The next two sentences reject two accounts, pressure melting (a person exerts too little pressure) and frictional heating (slipperiness remains constant across sliding speeds). The last sentence presents Bonn’s proposal as “more promising.” Choice B gives these three moves in order.

D.why_wrong: Bonn’s experiments are offered as evidence against frictional heating, not as proof of his own proposal, which the text calls only “more promising.”

I love all beauteous things,

Remembered on waking.

The following text is from John Galt’s 1821 novel Annals of the Parish. The narrator, a Scottish minister, records the events of 1778.

It was clear to me that the wars were not to be soon over; for I noticed, in the course of this year, that there was a greater christening of lad bairns than had ever been in any year during my incumbency; and grave and wise persons, observant of the signs of the times, said, that it had been long held as a sure prognostication of war, when the births of male children outnumbered that of females.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray the narrator confidently judging how long a war will last from local signs that he and his neighbors trust
To show the narrator’s worry that the boys being born in the parish will one day be sent away to fight
To convey the narrator’s doubts about a prediction offered by older and more respected members of the parish
To explain how the outbreak of a war had led to an unusual increase in the number of children born and christened in the parish
items.explanation: The narrator says it was “clear” to him that the wars would not soon be over, because more boys were christened that year than in any other during his time as minister, and “grave and wise persons” held that more male than female births was a “sure prognostication of war.” The text thus portrays him confidently judging how long the war will last from a local sign that he and others in the parish trust, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text does connect the boys’ births to the war, but only as a sign of how long the war will last; the narrator never worries that these boys will have to fight.

C.why_wrong: The narrator does not doubt the “grave and wise persons”: he reports their saying as support for what was already “clear” to him.

D.why_wrong: The text treats the many male births as a sign that foretells war, not as a result of the war; it gives no cause for the births at all.

It provides an estimate of the number of laborers that the text goes on to question on the grounds that company records undercount them.

The next sentence turns (“Yet”) to the fact that not a single diary or letter by any of these workers has been recovered. items.passage: Begun in 1856 to measure how various fertilizers affect hay yields, the Park Grass Experiment at Rothamsted in England is the oldest ecological experiment still running. Because its plots have received largely the same treatments year after year, the experiment has gradually addressed questions its founders never anticipated. In the 1970s, researchers found that sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum) on neighboring plots had evolved distinct adaptations to the soil conditions that the treatments had produced, one of the first demonstrations of evolution on so small a scale.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how fertilizer treatments at Rothamsted raised hay yields and why English farmers adopted them
To describe a long-running field experiment and show how it has come to serve purposes beyond its original one
To argue that experiments become more valuable the longer their treatments remain unchanged
To describe a long-running field experiment and explain why its founders chose to keep each plot’s treatment the same from year to year
items.explanation: The text introduces the Park Grass Experiment, begun in 1856 to test fertilizers’ effects on hay, and notes that because its plots have been treated in largely the same way for so long, it has addressed questions its founders “never anticipated.” The example of sweet vernal grass evolving on neighboring plots shows one such new use. Choice B states this purpose: the text describes the experiment and shows how it came to serve purposes beyond its original one.

A.recipe: original purpose taken as the topic (PART/INV)
A.why_wrong: The experiment was begun to test fertilizers on hay, but the text reports no yields and says nothing about farmers; it moves at once to the questions the experiment later answered.

C.recipe: one stated reason turned into a general argument (STANCE/BROAD)
C.why_wrong: The text does link the experiment’s later uses to its long-standing treatments, but only to describe this one experiment; it makes no general argument about how experiments should be run.

D.recipe: first clause right, founders’ reason invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text does describe a long-running experiment, but it never gives the founders’ reasons for their design; it says only what the long-standing treatments later made possible, questions the founders “never anticipated.”

sources.what: Silvertown et al. 2006, Journal of Ecology: the Park Grass Experiment, begun in 1856, is the oldest ecological experiment in existence; its value to science has grown since it was founded to answer agricultural questions; it provided one of the first demonstrations of the evolution of adaptation at a very local scale

items.passage: When Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff, and Stefan Schmukle analyzed personality data from more than 20,000 adults in Germany, the United States, and Great Britain, firstborns and later-borns proved virtually indistinguishable in extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness, and conscientiousness; only in self-reported intellect did firstborns score slightly higher. The results sit uneasily with a long-popular belief that a child’s place among siblings shapes character in lasting ways. That belief, the data suggest, holds at most for intellectual traits, and even there the difference is slight.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To present research suggesting that a widely held idea about how family position affects personality is largely mistaken
To report a study showing that birth order affects personality more strongly in Germany than in the United States or Great Britain
To explain why firstborns tend to report higher levels of intellect than their younger siblings do
To report research in order to show that birth order shapes intellectual traits as strongly as many people believe it shapes character
items.explanation: The text reports that in data from more than 20,000 adults, firstborns and later-borns were “virtually indistinguishable” in four major personality traits, with only a slight difference in self-reported intellect. It then says the results “sit uneasily” with the popular belief that birth order shapes character and that the belief holds “at most” for intellectual traits, where the difference is slight. Choice A states this purpose: the text presents research suggesting that a common idea is largely mistaken.

B.why_wrong: The study drew on adults from all three countries, but the text reports its results for the whole sample and never compares the countries.

C.recipe: one detail taken as the purpose (PART)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions that firstborns scored slightly higher in self-reported intellect but offers no explanation for it; the difference is a minor qualification, not the point of the text.

D.why_wrong: The text does report research and does find an effect only for intellectual traits, but it calls that effect slight; it never says birth order shapes intellect strongly.

items.passage: Tikvah Alper, a South African–born physicist, became a leading British radiobiologist through her studies of how radiation damages living cells. In the 1960s she and her colleagues turned this expertise on scrapie, a fatal brain disease of sheep, exposing infected tissue to radiation that would have inactivated a virus. The tissue remained infectious. By suggesting that the disease agent might lack nucleic acid altogether, the result helped prepare the way for the prion theory, which attributes such diseases to abnormal proteins.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a researcher, describes an experiment she carried out, and then explains why later scientists rejected the experiment’s result.
It introduces a researcher, describes how she developed a treatment for a disease of animals, and then notes how widely that treatment came to be used.
It describes a disease of sheep, explains how a researcher identified its cause, and then presents the theory that she later proposed to account for the disease.
It introduces a scientist, describes how she applied her expertise to an unfamiliar problem, and then suggests why the outcome mattered for later research.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Tikvah Alper and her field, the study of how radiation damages cells. The next two sentences describe how she and her colleagues applied that expertise to scrapie, irradiating infected tissue that nonetheless stayed infectious. The last sentence explains the result’s importance: by suggesting the agent might lack nucleic acid, it helped prepare the way for the prion theory. Choice D gives these three moves in order.

A.why_wrong: The text does introduce Alper and describe her experiment, but it says the result helped prepare the way for a later theory, not that scientists rejected it.

B.why_wrong: Alper exposed infected tissue to radiation to learn about the disease agent; the text mentions no treatment, so there is nothing whose use could spread.

C.why_wrong: The result only suggested what the agent might lack, and the prion theory is described as a later theory her result helped prepare the way for, not one she proposed.

sources.what: Tikvah Alper: South African-born physicist and radiobiologist in Britain; with colleagues (Nature 1967) found that radiation did not kill the scrapie agent, among the first evidence that the agent does not contain nucleic acid; the finding was instrumental in the development of the prion theory, which posits a rogue protein

items.passage: Analyzing the annual growth rings of Great Basin bristlecone pines (Pinus longaeva) from three mountain ranges in California and Nevada, Matthew Salzer and colleagues found that trees within about 150 meters of the upper treeline grew more after 1950 than in any other fifty-year interval of the past 3,700 years, a surge they attribute to rising temperatures, since cold constrains growth at such elevations. Rocky Mountain bristlecone pines near their upper limit have exhibited comparable increases. Bristlecones growing farther downslope, however, displayed no such surge: there, moisture rather than cold restricts growth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

It reports a finding about one group of trees, notes a similar result in a related species, and then predicts that trees farther downslope will soon show the same surge.

It reports a finding and offers an explanation for it, notes that other researchers have disputed that explanation, and then describes a study designed to settle the matter.

B.why_wrong: The text makes no prediction about the downslope trees; it explains that they showed no surge because moisture, not cold, limits their growth there.

D.why_wrong: No one in the text disputes the temperature explanation, and no study is designed to settle a dispute; the second sentence reports a similar finding elsewhere.

sources.what: Salzer, Hughes, Bunn and Kipfmueller 2009 (PNAS): bristlecone pines within about 150 m of upper treeline in three ranges of eastern California and Nevada grew more in the second half of the 20th century than in any 50-year period in 3,700 years; rising temperatures at high elevations are the likely cause, as cold limits growth there; at lower elevations growth is limited more by moisture; the same pattern has been seen in Rocky Mountain bristlecone pines

She turned away abruptly, and looked toward the corner where Billy slept on a pallet. The blankets on his bed were insufficient even for him. To illustrate how Jim’s illness has spread to his younger sisters and brother

items.passage: Analyzing sediments from the Corriental reservoir, which once supplied drinking water to the Maya city of Tikal in present-day Guatemala, Kenneth Tankersley and colleagues identified zeolite and quartz sand transported from ridges about 18 miles away. The system is the first of its kind documented in the ancient Americas, preceding comparable European filtration by nearly two millennia.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes how researchers made a discovery at an ancient site, then explains how the discovery led them to revise an earlier hypothesis.
It describes how researchers analyzed sediments from an ancient reservoir, then explains why their conclusions about it remain uncertain.
It explains how researchers reached a conclusion about an ancient practice, then indicates why that practice is notable.
It presents a theory about how an ancient city obtained clean water, then describes evidence that weakens that theory.
items.explanation: The first two sentences explain how Tankersley’s team reached its conclusion: they found zeolite and quartz, minerals that act as a natural sieve, in the reservoir’s sediments and concluded that the Maya used them to filter water. The last sentence says why this matters: the system is the first of its kind observed in the ancient Americas and predates similar European systems by nearly two millennia. A.why_wrong: The text does describe a discovery at an ancient site, but it mentions no earlier hypothesis; the last sentence explains why the filter is notable.

B.why_wrong: The researchers did analyze the reservoir’s sediments, but the text presents their conclusion with confidence and never calls it uncertain.

D.why_wrong: No theory is weakened: the text reports evidence for a conclusion, that the Maya filtered their water, and then explains its importance.

sources.what: Tankersley et al. 2020 (Scientific Reports), University of Cincinnati release: zeolite and quartz at Tikal’s Corriental reservoir formed a natural molecular sieve filtering drinking water; minerals from ridges about 18 miles away; the Maya used it more than 2,000 years ago; first observed in the ancient New World; predates similar European systems by nearly 2,000 years

items.passage: In 1960, a group of young Japanese architects who called themselves the Metabolists argued that buildings and cities should be able to renew themselves the way living organisms do, replacing worn-out parts while the whole lives on. Kisho Kurokawa’s Nakagin Capsule Tower, an apartment building completed in Tokyo in 1972, gave this idea a concrete form. The building’s 140 prefabricated apartments were capsules attached by high-tension bolts to two concrete towers, so that each could be detached and replaced with a new one as it aged.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes a disagreement among a group of architects and then explains how one building settled it.
The text presents a view of how buildings should function and then describes a building designed around that view.
The text outlines a theory of architecture and then describes a building whose design departed from that theory in important ways.
The text presents a view of how buildings should function and then explains why that view was abandoned once a building based on it was finished.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents the Metabolists’ idea that buildings and cities should renew themselves like living organisms, replacing worn-out parts. The rest of the text describes Kurokawa’s Nakagin Capsule Tower, whose capsules were bolted on so that each could be detached and replaced, a building designed to put that idea into practice. Choice B describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The Metabolists are presented as sharing one idea, not disagreeing, and the building applies their idea rather than settling a dispute.

C.why_wrong: The tower “gave this idea a concrete form”: its replaceable capsules follow the theory rather than departing from it.

D.why_wrong: The text does present the Metabolists’ view, but it never says the view was abandoned; it ends by describing how the tower’s design reflects it.

sources.what: Nakagin Capsule Tower (Iconic Houses): a representative work of Metabolism, the idea that buildings should be renewable; designed by Kisho Kurokawa, completed in Tokyo in 1972; 140 capsule apartments on two interconnected concrete towers, connected by high-tension bolts so they could be replaced as they aged; no capsule was ever replaced

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (architecture). Key B. Modeled on 2.10 (a philosophy, then a work influenced by it). The passage says only that each capsule could be replaced, not that any was (none ever was, and the tower was demolished in 2022), so it does not imply replacement. The Metabolist manifesto was presented in 1960 at the World Design Conference in Tokyo. A is a wholly wrong template; C and D keep the first move’s subject and fail in the second. Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage: For most of the history of the transatlantic slave trade, captives’ names went unrecorded once they were forced aboard ship, making it difficult to know where in Africa they had come from. After Britain outlawed the trade in 1807, however, courts in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and Havana, Cuba, registered the names of Africans freed from intercepted ships. Historian David Eltis and his colleagues have put these names online, asking people who recognize a name to identify the language and culture it belongs to, and so its bearer’s likely homeland.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It points out a limitation of early slave-trade records, then explains that courts were created in the 1800s specifically to correct it.
It describes how courts in two cities recorded the names of freed Africans, then explains why those records were long kept secret.
It explains why the origins of many enslaved Africans are hard to trace, then argues that historians should stop relying on names to trace them.
It identifies a difficulty in learning about certain people’s origins, then describes a project designed to overcome it.
items.explanation: The first sentence states the problem: captives’ names went unrecorded once they were forced aboard ship, so it is hard to know where in Africa they came from. The rest of the text describes Eltis’s approach: using names registered by courts after 1807 and asking people who recognize a name to identify its language and culture, and so its bearer’s likely homeland. Choice D gives these two moves.

A.why_wrong: The courts did register names, but they handled Africans freed from intercepted ships after the trade was outlawed; nothing says they were created to fix gaps in the records.

B.why_wrong: The courts’ registers are one part of the text, not its opening problem, and nothing suggests they were kept secret; Eltis’s team has put the names online.

C.why_wrong: The text does explain why origins are hard to trace, but the names are the solution it describes, not something historians should abandon.

sources.what: African Origins project (Emory): for most of the slave trade, captives’ names were lost once they were forced aboard; after the trade was outlawed in 1807, courts intercepting slave ships recorded their names; visitors who recognize a name identify the modern country, language and culture that use it; David Eltis leads the project

items.notes: Area: history. Key D. A and C keep move 1 and break move 2. Own blind solve before review: D.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Henry Lawson’s 1897 poem “The Uncultured Rhymer to His Cultured Critics.”

You were quick to pick on a faulty line
That I strove to put my soul in:
Your eyes were keen for a ‘dash’ of mine
In the place of a semi-colon—
And blind to the rest. And is it for such
As you I must brook restriction?
‘I was taught too little?’ I learnt too much
To care for a pedant’s diction!

Must I turn aside from my destined way
For a task your Joss [idol] would find me?
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker responds to critics who fault his writing, then insists that he will keep to his own chosen path.
The speaker admits that his lack of schooling has weakened his poems, then asks his critics to help him improve them.
The speaker praises his critics for their careful reading, then explains why he has decided to accept their advice.
The speaker recalls a disagreement about punctuation, then predicts that his critics will soon change their opinion of his work.
items.explanation: In the first stanza the speaker answers critics who seized on “a faulty line” and a dash used in place of a semicolon while staying “blind to the rest,” and he turns their charge that he was “taught too little” back on them. In the last lines he asks whether he must “turn aside from my destined way” for a task they would set him, a question that insists he will not. The poem responds to criticism of his writing and then affirms his commitment to his own course, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: “I was taught too little?” repeats the critics’ charge as a question, and he answers that he “learnt too much / To care for a pedant’s diction”; he concedes nothing and asks for no help.

C.why_wrong: Their eyes were “keen” only for small faults and “blind to the rest”; this is a complaint, and he refuses their advice rather than accepting it.

D.why_wrong: The dash and semicolon are one example of the critics’ fault-finding, and the speaker makes no prediction about their opinions; he says he will not turn aside from his own way.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Verses Popular and Humorous, 1900, pp. 111–112); the poem first appeared in The Bulletin, 25 December 1897, per AustLit and the Coolabah article on Lawson and John Le Gay Brereton
Barnes, “An uncultured rhymer and his cultured critics” (Coolabah 2014): the poem dated 1897, written to John Le Gay Brereton after his comment on Lawson’s prosody

The ambition move is a commitment (“Must I turn aside from my destined way”), so the key says “keep to his own chosen path,” not a grand ambition. Length 97 words with the attribution (2.21: 100). Own blind solve before review: A.

items.passage: Why is the skin of the African elephant (Loxodonta africana) crisscrossed by an intricate network of minuscule channels? Using microscopy and computer simulations, Michel Milinkovitch and colleagues determined that the channels are fractures in the skin’s brittle outer layer, which elephants do not shed in the usual way. As that layer progressively thickens over the tiny elevations covering the skin, bending stress accumulates in the valleys between them until the layer cracks. The researchers suggest that these fractures benefit the animals: the channels retain water, which helps elephants stay cool, and help mud adhere to the skin, protecting it from intense sunlight and parasites.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text raises a question about elephants, then explains why researchers have so far been unable to answer it.
The text describes a common belief about elephants, then presents evidence showing that the belief is mistaken.
The text poses a question about a physical feature of an animal, then presents a research team’s explanation for it.
The text asks why an animal’s skin looks the way it does, then compares that skin with the skin of other large mammals.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: why is the African elephant’s skin crisscrossed by tiny channels? The rest presents Milinkovitch’s team’s answer: the channels are cracks in the brittle outer layer, formed as it thickens and bends over the skin’s bumps, and they help the animals by holding water and mud. Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The question is answered: the researchers explain how the channels form and how they may help elephants.

B.why_wrong: The text begins with a question, not a belief, and nothing in it is shown to be mistaken.

D.why_wrong: The text says elephants do not shed the outer layer “in the usual way,” but it never compares their skin with that of any other large mammal.

sources.what: Martins, Milinkovitch et al. 2018 (Nature Communications), University of Geneva release: the minuscule crevices on African elephant skin are true fractures of the brittle, shedding-deficient outer layer, caused by bending stress in the valleys between millimetric elevations; they retain 5 to 10 times more water than flat skin; mud protects against parasites

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology, biomechanics). Key C. Modeled on 2.24 (a question, then a possible answer). The source names António Martins as first author and Michel Milinkovitch as leader; the passage names Milinkovitch “and colleagues.” Sun protection is in the paper’s abstract (protection against parasites and intense solar radiation by mud adherence). Options vary their openings so that no three share one long prefix; A and D keep move 1 and break move 2. Own blind solve before review: C.

The following text is from Fanny Fern’s 1854 novel Ruth Hall. Ruth and her husband are spending the summer at a resort hotel called Beach Cliff.

<u>Hotel life is about the same in every latitude.</u> At Beach Cliff there was the usual number of vapid, fashionable mothers; dressy, brainless daughters; half-fledged wine-bibbing sons; impudent, whisker-dyed roués; bachelors, anxious to give their bashfulness an airing; bronchial clergymen, in search of health and a text; waning virgins, languishing by candle-light; gouty uncles, dyspeptic aunts, whist-playing old ladies, flirting nursery maids and neglected children.
items.stem: Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence in the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a setting that the following sentence goes on to describe in terms of its natural surroundings.
It offers a generalization that the following sentence illustrates with the guests at one hotel.
It establishes a contrast with the description of the hotel’s guests in the following sentence.
It summarizes the narrator’s praise for Beach Cliff, which the following sentence elaborates on.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence makes a general claim: hotel life is the same everywhere. The next sentence bears it out with a list of the “usual” guests at Beach Cliff, from fashionable mothers and brainless daughters to gouty uncles and neglected children. So the underlined sentence offers a generalization that the following sentence illustrates, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The following sentence does describe Beach Cliff, but through the people staying there, not through any natural surroundings.

C.why_wrong: The list of “the usual number” of familiar types confirms that hotel life is the same everywhere; it does not contrast with the underlined claim.

D.why_wrong: The guests are described mockingly (“vapid,” “brainless,” “whisker-dyed”); neither sentence praises Beach Cliff.

The following text is from George Madden Martin’s 1902 novel Emmy Lou: Her Book and Heart. Emmy Lou, a schoolgirl, has been seated away from her friend Hattie by their teacher.

And so Emmy Lou and Hattie were separated. But there were three new little girls near Emmy Lou. Their kid button-shoes had tassels. Very few little girls had button-shoes. Button-shoes were new. Emmy Lou had button-shoes. She was proud of them. <u>But they did not have tassels.</u>

items.passage: Clementine Hunter spent most of her life on Melrose Plantation in Louisiana, where she picked cotton and later worked as a cook and laundress. Although she did not begin painting until approximately age fifty, she produced more than five thousand works, many depicting the agricultural labor, religious ceremonies, and social gatherings of the Black community along the Cane River. To explain how Hunter’s painting style changed after her 1955 exhibition
To give an overview of Hunter’s life and work and an important recognition she received
To compare Hunter’s paintings of Cane River life with those of other Louisiana artists
items.explanation: The text describes Hunter’s working life on Melrose Plantation, her start as a painter at about fifty, the thousands of works she produced and their subjects, and her 1955 solo exhibition at the Delgado Museum, the first there for an African American artist. Norah turned from the creek and entered the scrub. She loved the bush, and was never happier than when exploring its recesses. To convey Norah’s delight in the bush and her natural skill at moving through it
To describe Norah’s fear of getting lost in an unfamiliar place
To show that Norah would rather explore alone than spend time with her family

Ranald always hated new clothes. He felt them an intolerable burden. He did not mind his new homespun, home-made flannel check shirt of mixed red and white, but the heavy fulled-cloth suit made by his Aunt Kirsty felt like a suit of mail. items.passage: Some musicians and scientists have converted climate measurements into music, hoping that listeners will grasp through sound what conventional graphs struggle to communicate. <u>In 2013, Daniel Crawford, then a student at the University of Minnesota, composed a piece for cello in which each note represents one year from 1880 to 2012, with higher pitches corresponding to warmer global temperatures.</u> Performed in sequence, the notes gradually ascend as the planet warms.

It explains why graphs are a poor way to present scientific data.
It describes how Crawford first became interested in climate science.
It presents a criticism of using music to communicate scientific information.

items.passage: Conservation laws usually protect two kinds of living things: plants and animals. Fungi, which make up a separate biological kingdom, typically receive no mention, even though they decompose organic material into soil and help many plants absorb water and nutrients. Largely through the advocacy of mycologist Giuliana Furci, Chile became the first country to protect fungi by law. Other nations should follow its example.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how fungi help plants absorb water and nutrients
To argue that fungi deserve a place in efforts to protect living things
To describe how Chile’s environmental laws have changed over the past century
To question whether fungi should be considered a separate kingdom of life
items.explanation: The text says conservation laws usually protect only plants and animals and leave out fungi, although fungi do important work, and it calls conservation that ignores them “incomplete.” It points to Chile as the first country to protect fungi by law and ends, “Other nations should follow its example.” The text argues that fungi should be included in conservation, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that fungi help plants absorb water and nutrients only as a reason fungi deserve protection; it does not explain how they do it.

C.why_wrong: Chile is mentioned once, as an example for other nations; the text gives no history of its laws.

D.why_wrong: The text states that fungi make up a kingdom of their own; it does not question it.

items.notes: Area: natural science (conservation policy). Key B, paraphrased (“deserve a place in efforts to protect”). Modeled on 1.22 (an argument with an explicit evaluative close). The year of Chile’s law is left out (sources give 2012 to 2014). Own blind solve before review: B.

It presents a claim that the rest of the sentence goes on to support with additional evidence.
It describes the main goal of the study introduced in the first sentence.
It gives background that helps show why the comparison in the rest of the sentence matters.

items.explanation: The text introduces Himid and the main concern of her work, Black people whom European art and history have overlooked, and then describes Naming the Money as an example of that concern. Choice A describes this structure.

items.passage: In the centuries before 1000 CE, the island of Helgö, in a lake in eastern Sweden, was a flourishing center of commerce and metalworking with connections extending to distant regions. Among the artifacts recovered there is <u>a bronze statuette of the Buddha, probably manufactured in the late 400s or early 500s in the Swat Valley, in present-day Pakistan</u>. Archaeologists excavating the site also uncovered a bishop’s staff from Ireland and a bronze vessel from Egypt.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why metalworkers on the island made statues of the Buddha.
It describes how the island’s trade with Ireland and Egypt began.
It shows that the island had become an important center of Buddhist worship in Sweden.
It gives one piece of evidence that the island had links to faraway places.
items.explanation: The first sentence says Helgö had “connections extending to distant regions.” The underlined portion gives evidence of those connections: a statuette of the Buddha made thousands of kilometers away, in the Swat Valley. The final sentence adds more such objects.

A.why_wrong: The statuette was probably made in the Swat Valley, not by metalworkers on Helgö.

B.why_wrong: Ireland and Egypt come up only in the final sentence, which lists other objects found at the site; the text says nothing about how that trade began.

C.why_wrong: One statuette shows a connection to a distant place; the text says nothing about Buddhist worship on the island.

Wikipedia, Helgö: the old trading town on Helgö in Lake Mälaren, settled from about 200 AD; finds include a small Buddha figure (6th century), an Irish crozier head and a Coptic scoop from Egypt

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). Key D. Easy F_example on the model of 1.3 (an example of the claim in the first sentence). Helgö is in Lake Mälaren. Wikipedia names Kashmir as a possible origin beside Swat, hence “probably.” Own blind solve: D.

items.passage: Many picture books for young children depict animals wearing clothes and talking like people. Psychologist Patricia Ganea and her colleagues investigated whether such books influence what children learn about real animals. They read three- to five-year-olds a book about an unfamiliar animal; some children heard it described in factual language, while others heard it described as talking and having humanlike intentions. Children of every age in the second group were afterward more likely to attribute human characteristics to real animals, even though the book’s pictures had been realistic.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains why authors of children’s picture books often show animals wearing clothes.
It describes a study of how one feature of children’s books affects what young readers learn.
It argues that preschoolers should not be allowed to read books in which animals talk.
It compares how children and adults respond to books about animals they have never seen.
items.explanation: The text describes research on whether books that present animals as humanlike change what children learn: some children heard a factual description of an animal and others a humanlike one, and the second group more often attributed human characteristics to real animals. Choice B states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text notes that such books are common but gives no reason why authors write them.

C.why_wrong: The text reports findings; it makes no recommendation about what preschoolers should read.

D.why_wrong: The study involved only three- to five-year-olds; no adults took part.

sources.what: Ganea, Canfield, Simons-Ghafari and Chou 2014, Frontiers in Psychology: Study 1, 3- to 5-year-olds saw realistic drawings of a novel animal with factual or anthropomorphic language; children in all age groups more often attributed human traits to real animals after anthropomorphic language (language did not change fact learning in Study 1; fewer facts were learned only when pictures and language were both anthropomorphic, Study 2)

items.notes: Area: social science (developmental psychology). Key B. Easy P_study on the model of 1.15 (presents a study that addresses a question). The passage describes Study 1, where humanlike language raised attribution of human traits at every age but did not change fact learning (the reviewer removed a clause saying the younger children learned fewer facts). Own blind solve: B.

fixes: passage overstated the source: in the study described (Study 1, realistic pictures, factual or humanlike language) language did not change how many facts children learned (Table 1 and ANOVA); fewer facts were learned only in Study 2, with humanlike pictures too. items.passage: When water runs short, plants compete for it, yet some trees supply water to their neighbors. In a 1993 study, ecologist Todd Dawson found that sugar maples perform <u>what scientists call “hydraulic lift”</u> during droughts. At night, the trees’ deep roots absorb groundwater from saturated soil far below the surface, and their shallow roots release some of it into the parched upper layers. Every neighboring plant Dawson examined consumed some of this redistributed water, and those that depended on it most grew more vigorously than plants that used little or none.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a term for a process that the following sentence explains.
It presents a hypothesis that Dawson’s results went on to disprove.
It describes a problem that sugar maples cause for the plants around them.
It explains why Dawson chose to study sugar maples rather than other trees.
items.explanation: The underlined portion gives the name scientists use, “hydraulic lift,” and the next sentence explains the process: deep roots take up water at night and shallow roots release some of it into the parched upper soil. Choice A describes this function.

B.why_wrong: The underlined portion names a process Dawson found, and the rest of the text describes it; nothing is disproved.

C.why_wrong: The text says neighboring plants consumed the lifted water and grew more vigorously, so the maples help rather than harm them.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say why Dawson chose sugar maples.

sources.what: Dawson 1993, Oecologia, abstract: sugar maple shows hydraulic lift during drought, nocturnal uptake of water from deep soil released from shallow roots into upper soil layers; all neighbors used some fraction (3 to 60 percent) of the lifted water; neighbors using a high proportion grew more

items.notes: Area: natural science (plant ecology). Key A. Easy F_term on the model of 1.11, built differently: the term arrives inside a research finding in sentence 2, and the explanation follows. Own blind solve: A.

fixes: opening 'Plants in dry environments' changed: Dawson’s own conclusion is that hydraulic lift matters in relatively mesic sites under periodic drought
